paras: The lynching of Frank Brown, called Jim Brown in Bossier Parish papers, was the hanging of a Black plantation worker by a posse of white men near McDade station in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on the morning of February 24, 1903. Brown was accused of shooting the overseer Harvey Connell, who was not seriously hurt, and of firing at the plantation's owner, McDade, during a dispute over work. A brief Shreveport dispatch carried the killing to papers across the country, while the Caucasian printed a long account that defended the lynchers.

According to the Caucasian, Brown lived in a cabin on the old Knox Point plantation in Bossier, about twenty miles below Shreveport, where he was employed. Wire dispatches placed the killing at McDade, a station on the Shreveport and Red River Valley Railroad about twelve miles from Shreveport.

The Caucasian, summarizing what it called "a long drawn out statement," said that shortly after 6 o'clock on Tuesday morning Connell woke Brown, who replied that he would not go to work because his brother was in trouble. McDade then had Connell bring Brown to the lot to be paid off, and when McDade "upbraided him for his laziness," Brown was said to have answered with "impudent words." In this version the two men began struggling, and Brown, holding a revolver, shot Connell in the forearm and the leg, fired at McDade and ran, and Connell shot him in the leg as he fled. The wire dispatches gave a shorter account in which McDade and Brown "had a dispute about work," Connell "interfered," and Brown shot him twice.

A posse of white men was organized and, "after a brisk ride," captured and disarmed Brown and hanged him to a tree near McDade station, about half a mile from where Connell had been shot. The New York Sun's New Orleans dispatch said simply that "a mob promptly lynched him," and the Waxahachie Daily Light's Shreveport dispatch credited the hanging to "infuriated citizens." Connell was taken to Shreveport for treatment and was reported not badly wounded.

Nine days later the Bossier Banner recorded the lynching in a single sentence among its local items, giving the charge as "assaulting Mr. J. T. McDade with intent to murder." No report of an inquest, arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial appears in the coverage. The killing was later counted in tallies of the year's lynchings, listed by the Indianapolis Journal as "Frank Brown, colored, McDade, La." and by the Sedalia Times as a lynching for murder at "McDade Ga."

The first reports came from a Shreveport dispatch of February 24, run that day by the San Antonio Daily Light and the next morning by the Indianapolis Journal (which gave the station as "McReade") and the New-York Tribune, saying only that Brown "shot a man named Connell, but not fatally." The Tribune set the item beside the killing of William Fambro by a mob at Griffin, Georgia, under the ironic headline "The Best Friend of the Negro" and the subhead "Southern Whites' Way of Proving Their Defenders' Assertion." Over the next two weeks weekly news digests in Minnesota, Michigan and Arkansas reprinted one-sentence versions, some identifying Brown only as a man "who shot a white man."

Closer to the scene, the Caucasian ran its account under the headlines "A Negro Lynched" and "He Was Pulled to the Limb of a Tree," and printed it again the following day. The paper described Brown as "shiftless and a disturber of the peace" and wrote that "the outraged citizens became the judge, the jury and the executioner," calling such action "not surprising" when "a desperate and lawless man" threatened a community.

In the Black press, the Richmond Planet printed the wire item without comment in its news summary for Wednesday, February 25. In August the Sedalia Times included Brown in a "Record of Lynching" for the first half of 1903, drawn from a count of men "laid ta rest in silent tomb" kept by the Striker. No Black-press editorial on the case was found.

The victim was named Frank Brown in the wire reports and the Black press, but Jim Brown in the two local papers, the Caucasian and the Bossier Banner. Most reports placed the lynching early on February 24, a Tuesday by the local papers' reckoning, while the Sun's New Orleans dispatch of that date said it had occurred "yesterday." Accounts also differed on the distance from Shreveport, about twelve miles in the wire dispatches and about twenty in the Caucasian; the owner's name appeared as Tom McDade and J. T. McDade, and the overseer's as Connell and "Cornell."

reader.title: Lynching of Frank Brown
bases: A posse or mob of white men pursued, captured and hanged Brown after he was accused of shooting the plantation overseer (A6, A4, A5).

Brown was hanged without any legal process by 'a posse of white men' (A6), 'a mob' (A4) or 'infuriated citizens' (A5), a group of unstated but plural size, for shooting Connell; the Caucasian said the citizens acted as 'the judge, the jury and the executioner' (A6).
Two local papers (A6, A13) and an independent Shreveport/New Orleans wire (A1, A4, A5) agree that Brown was lynched near McDade station on Feb. 24 after shooting Connell.

accounts.label: New Orleans/Shreveport wire
accounts.gist: McDade and Brown had a dispute about work, young Harvey Connell interfered and Brown shot him twice; a mob or 'infuriated citizens' promptly lynched him.

accounts.gist: Frank Brown was lynched at McDade station early in the morning for shooting Connell, not fatally.

accounts.label: Bossier Banner
accounts.gist: Jim Brown was lynched at Knox Point for assaulting J. T. McDade with intent to murder and shooting Harvey Cornell.

framing.detail: The Caucasian called Brown 'shiftless and a disturber of the peace' and the lynching 'not surprising' given 'a desperate and lawless man'.
The New-York Tribune ran the item under "The Best Friend of the Negro" / "Southern Whites' Way of Proving Their Defenders' Assertion."
Most papers printed one-sentence wire or digest items; several described Brown only as a negro 'who shot a white man'.
The Bossier Banner gave a one-sentence local item stating the charge.
The Richmond Planet printed the wire item without comment; the Sedalia Times counted it in a year's lynching list.
